screens.title: What is a Game Object (Entity)?
screens.narratorSegment: A game object, often called an entity, is any item in the game world that stores data or exhibits behavior you care about. That includes obvious actors like the player and enemies, interactive pickups like health packs or weapons, static scenery if you need to render or collide with it, and even invisible managers such as an audio controller. The essential property is that the object may need Update or Render calls during the game loop. A practical example is a treasure chest: it needs a PositionComponent to know where it sits, a RenderComponent to draw the sprite, and perhaps an InteractionComponent to open and grant loot. A common misconception is thinking every object must be a full class with its own methods. Instead, treating a game object as a thin container simplifies extension: add components for new features rather than altering a monolithic class. This definition grounds the rest of the chapter because our goal is to create a small, consistent container type to which components attach. Keep in mind: deciding whether something is a game object depends on whether it needs to be managed each frame; if not, it may be plain data rather than an entity.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › What is a Game Object
Definition & examples
  • Player character with input and health.
  • Enemies with AI, position, and render components.
  • Pickups like Health Packs with position and value data.
  • Static objects when they need collision or rendering.
Key Takeaway

If it needs Update or Render, model it as a GameObject with components rather than ad-hoc globals.

Analogy

screens.title: Composition vs Inheritance
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance gives a natural “is-a” relationship, which is useful in many domains. In games, however, inheritance often creates brittle trees: a Player needs inventory, an Enemy needs AI, and a Tree might need collision. If you rely on inheritance, you quickly face either duplication or a bloated base class that tries to do everything. Composition solves this by attaching small, focused components to a generic GameObject container. For example, a Player can have Position, Render, Input, and Health components while a Tree only has Position and Render. The advantage is flexibility: add a Flight component and any entity can fly without changing an inheritance hierarchy. A common disadvantage is the need for component lookup and interaction: for instance, MovementComponent must find PositionComponent to update coordinates. That adds some bookkeeping, like passing a parent pointer or using GetComponent checks. A balanced understanding is important: use composition for flexible, varied entities, but design clear interaction patterns so components can find and communicate with each other without fragile assumptions. Composition vs Inheritance means composition yields modular, reusable behavior; avoid deep inheritance that forces a monolithic base class or many specialized subclasses.. In practical terms, why composition avoids rigid class hierarchies in games. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Composition vs Inheritance
Inheritance (traditional OOP)
  • Good for strict "is-a" relationships
  • Can create deep, rigid hierarchies
  • Risk of bloated base classes or duplicated code
Misconception

Inheritance always simplifies code. In practice, it can make additions and cross-cutting features harder to maintain.

Composition (component pattern)
  • Assemble behaviors from reusable components
  • Mix-and-match components to create entities
  • Requires clear lookup/interaction strategies between components
Pro-tip

Design components to be small and single-purpose. Keep component APIs minimal to reduce coupling.

screens.title: Component Base Class in C++
screens.narratorSegment: A Component base class establishes the contract every concrete component follows. The example uses a virtual destructor so derived components clean up properly when deleted through a base pointer. It also defines virtual Update and Render functions; Update is usually pure virtual because most components implement per-frame logic, while Render can be optional. Finally, a GetTypeName method helps identify components when printing or logging. In C++ this base class is intentionally small to let concrete components focus on data and behavior. For instance, PositionComponent owns x and y coordinates and does not render, while RenderComponent holds a sprite name and implements Render. The code pattern uses std::unique_ptr to manage component lifetimes inside a GameObject, which prevents leaks and centralizes ownership. A common misconception is that components must be heavyweight objects; instead they should be minimal and composable. This makes memory management predictable and behavior easy to reuse across multiple GameObjects. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Component Base Class
Key points
  • Virtual destructor for polymorphic cleanup.
  • Update(double deltaTime) as the frame step.
  • Render is optional; not all components draw.
Example
class Component {
public:
  virtual ~Component() = default;
  virtual void Update(double deltaTime) = 0;
  virtual void Render() {}
  virtual const char* GetTypeName() const = 0;
};
Concrete components
PositionComponent: holds x, y and exposes Set/Get
RenderComponent: stores sprite name and draws it
HealthComponent: tracks health and provides TakeDamage

screens.title: GameObject: AddComponent and GetComponent
screens.narratorSegment: The GameObject in this chapter is intentionally simple: it owns a vector of std::unique_ptr and provides template helpers AddComponent and GetComponent. AddComponent constructs a new component using make_unique and returns a raw pointer for immediate use. GetComponent performs a linear search with dynamic_cast to find the first component of the requested type. This approach is easy to implement and clear to read. The trade-off is lookup cost; for many objects and frequent lookups you may add a type-indexed map, but for beginners this simple pattern is instructive. Using unique_ptr means components are owned exclusively by their GameObject and automatically deallocated when the GameObject is destroyed or removed from the world. A common mistake is storing raw pointers to components elsewhere without clear ownership; that can produce dangling pointers after cleanup. Prefer obtaining components through GetComponent when needed and avoid storing raw pointers long-term unless you can guarantee lifetime. GameObject: AddComponent and GetComponent means store components in unique_ptr for exclusive ownership; use addcomponent/getcomponent templates to keep code generic and readable.. In practical terms, storing components with std::unique_ptr and simple lookup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › AddComponent / GetComponent
AddComponent pattern
template<typename T, typename... Args>
T* AddComponent(Args&&... args) {
  static_assert(std::is_base_of<Component, T>::value, "T must derive from Component");
  std::unique_ptr<T> newComponent = std::make_unique<T>(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
  T* rawPtr = newComponent.get();
  components_.push_back(std::move(newComponent));
  return rawPtr;
}
GetComponent lookup
template<typename T>
T* GetComponent() const {
  for (const auto& comp : components_) {
    if (dynamic_cast<T*>(comp.get())) {
      return static_cast<T*>(comp.get());
    }
  }
  return nullptr;
}
Note
This simple storage is clear and safe for ownership. If lookups become a bottleneck, add a type-indexed map or component registry for faster access.

screens.title: GameWorld / SceneManager
screens.narratorSegment: The GameWorld or SceneManager centralizes object lifecycle. It stores a container of GameObjects (usually std::vector of std::unique_ptr ), provides AddGameObject for new entities, and exposes UpdateAll and RenderAll to drive per-frame behavior. The typical frame flow is: add any pending objects, call UpdateAll with deltaTime so each GameObject updates its components, then call RenderAll to draw, and finally perform a cleanup pass to remove destroyed or dead objects. Cleanup is often deferred until after Update to avoid invalidating iterators or accessing freed objects mid-frame. In the example, CleanupDeadObjects removes objects whose HealthComponent reports IsDead. Using unique_ptr makes erasure and deallocation straightforward: when an element is removed from the vector the object's destructor runs. A frequent mistake is removing objects during the update loop itself, which can lead to skipped updates or invalid pointers. The safe pattern is to mark objects for deletion or check conditions and then erase them in a dedicated pass. GameWorld / SceneManager means update and render every frame, defer removals to a cleanup pass to keep iteration safe, and rely on smart pointers for automatic deallocation.. In practical terms, managing creation, update, render, and cleanup every frame. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › GameWorld / SceneManager
Game Loop Management
AddGameObject
Push a unique_ptr into the world container so ownership is clear and deletion automatic.
UpdateAll
Call Update(deltaTime) on each GameObject to progress simulation.
RenderAll
Call Render() so components that draw can produce visuals or console output for demos.
Cleanup pattern
void CleanupDeadObjects() {
  gameObjects_.erase(
    std::remove_if(gameObjects_.begin(), gameObjects_.end(),
      [](const std::unique_ptr<GameObject>& obj) {
        HealthComponent* health = obj->GetComponent<HealthComponent>();
        return health && health->IsDead();
      }),
    gameObjects_.end());
}

screens.title: Memory Safety with std::unique_ptr
screens.narratorSegment: Memory management is fundamental in C++ game code. Using std::unique_ptr for GameObject and Component ownership simplifies lifetime reasoning. A unique_ptr expresses exclusive ownership: when the container erases the unique_ptr, the pointed object is destroyed automatically. This removes much of the manual delete bookkeeping that causes leaks. In our example, components are stored as unique_ptr in a GameObject, and GameObjects themselves are held as unique_ptr inside GameWorld. The advantage is obvious when cleaning up: removing a GameObject from the vector deallocates its components and the object itself. A common mistake is keeping raw pointers to component memory elsewhere without updating them when objects are removed; these become dangling pointers. To avoid that, prefer querying components on demand with GetComponent, or if you must cache a pointer, ensure a clear ownership and lifetime contract, or use weak references in higher-level systems. For beginner projects this unique_ptr approach provides predictability while you design component interactions. Memory Safety with std::unique_ptr means use std::unique_ptr to make ownership explicit and automatic deallocation safe during cleanup.. In practical terms, why exclusive ownership avoids leaks and dangling pointers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Memory Safety
Unique ownership

Store components as std::unique_ptr<Component> inside GameObject and store GameObjects as std::unique_ptr<GameObject> in GameWorld. This makes deletion explicit when you erase elements from the container.

Benefit

Automatic destructor calls free resources and reduce leaks.

Watch out

Avoid storing raw pointers to component data outside ownership boundaries; prefer safe querying or clear lifetime documentation.

screens.title: Implementing MovementComponent (Activity)
screens.narratorSegment: The MovementComponent activity shows how components can interact: Movement finds the PositionComponent on its parent GameObject and updates coordinates using deltaTime. The step-by-step approach is to first provide a way for components to access their parent—either by passing the GameObject pointer into Update or by storing a parent pointer when the component is added. The example in the chapter modifies the Component's Update signature to accept a GameObject* parent, simplifying lookup. Implement Update to retrieve PositionComponent using GetComponent, check the returned pointer, then compute newX = currentX + directionX * speed * deltaTime, and set the new position. In main, add a MovementComponent to the Player with directionX = 1.0 to move right, run a few frames with a visible deltaTime, and print Position to confirm movement. A misconception to avoid: assuming movement will happen if PositionComponent is absent; always guard GetComponent results. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Movement Component
Steps

  2. Implement MovementComponent with speed and directionX/Y.
  3. In Update, call parent->GetComponent<PositionComponent>(); check for null.
  4. Compute new position using deltaTime and set it.

Starter snippet
class MovementComponent : public Component {
public:
  MovementComponent(float speed = 10.0f, float dirX = 0.0f, float dirY = 0.0f)
    : speed_(speed), directionX_(dirX), directionY_(dirY) {}

  void Update(double deltaTime, GameObject* parent) override {
    PositionComponent* pos = parent->GetComponent<PositionComponent>();
    if (pos) {
      pos->SetPosition(pos->GetX() + directionX_ * speed_ * deltaTime,
                       pos->GetY() + directionY_ * speed_ * deltaTime);
    }
  }
  // ...
};

screens.title: Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: As you build an entity system, three pitfalls recur. First, ownership confusion: storing raw pointers to components or GameObjects outside the owning container leads to dangling references when objects are deleted. The remedy is to rely on unique_ptr ownership and query components when needed. Second, unsafe lookups: calling GetComponent and using the result without checking for null is a common error. Always verify the pointer returned by GetComponent before accessing methods or data. Third, removing objects during iteration causes skipped updates, invalid iterators, or crashes. The recommended pattern is to perform a cleanup pass after Update and Render phases, erasing dead objects using remove_if on the world container. Additionally, be mindful that dynamic_cast-based lookups are simple but can be slow at scale; if you outgrow this pattern, consider a type-indexed registry or a full ECS. Addressing these issues early keeps your small engine predictable and easier to extend. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll build a clear mental model for what a game object is, why composition is preferred over inheritance in games, and how to manage many objects safely inside the game loop. A game object represents anything in your world that stores state or acts—players, enemies, items, scenery, or managers. The practical problem we solve is flexibility: how to give different entities different behavior without a huge rigid class tree. You'll see the component pattern as a simple, modular solution: components like Position, Render, and Health attach to a GameObject. We'll also examine how a GameWorld collects objects, calls Update and Render each frame, and safely removes dead objects using smart pointers. Throughout, concrete C++ examples illustrate AddComponent, GetComponent, Update loops, and cleanup logic. By the end you'll understand how to assemble entities from components, avoid a “God object” class, and use std::unique_ptr to avoid memory leaks. As you follow along, notice one common trap: components need a reliable way to find or talk to one another. Keep that question in mind as we implement and test a MovementComponent later.

These learning objectives capture the practical skills this chapter builds. First, you will define what a game object represents in a game engine context: any actor or item that stores data, responds to updates, or is rendered. Knowing that helps you decide which entities need components. Second, you'll understand composition over inheritance: instead of deep class trees, you will compose behavior from small components so entities remain flexible. Third, you'll implement a basic C++ GameObject class using a simplified component pattern. That includes writing a Component base class, concrete components like Position or Health, and AddComponent/GetComponent helpers. Finally, you'll manage a collection of game objects inside the game loop by creating a GameWorld or SceneManager which adds, updates, renders, and safely removes objects. Each objective is practical: defining entities prevents ad-hoc code, composition reduces coupling, implementation teaches ownership via std::unique_ptr, and world management avoids memory leaks and invalid pointers. These objectives are designed to equip you with a minimal, maintainable entity system you can extend in later chapters.

This second objectives slide expands the practical outcomes and highlights a hands-on activity. You will implement a MovementComponent that updates Position data and observe interactions when the GameWorld calls Update. This teaches component interaction: how one component locates and modifies another. The activity emphasizes a common pitfall: components often assume their sibling components exist. We'll discuss safe lookup patterns such as checking GetComponent results before use, and why storing a parent pointer or passing the parent to Update can be necessary. You will also practice using std::unique_ptr for ownership. That choice makes removal safe because deleting from the world vector deallocates the object automatically. Finally, we will test cleanup logic by simulating damage and removing dead objects. These exercises build a practical intuition about lifecycle, ownership, and inter-component communication, and give you concrete code you can reuse.

A game object, often called an entity, is any item in the game world that stores data or exhibits behavior you care about. That includes obvious actors like the player and enemies, interactive pickups like health packs or weapons, static scenery if you need to render or collide with it, and even invisible managers such as an audio controller. The essential property is that the object may need Update or Render calls during the game loop. A practical example is a treasure chest: it needs a PositionComponent to know where it sits, a RenderComponent to draw the sprite, and perhaps an InteractionComponent to open and grant loot. A common misconception is thinking every object must be a full class with its own methods. Instead, treating a game object as a thin container simplifies extension: add components for new features rather than altering a monolithic class. This definition grounds the rest of the chapter because our goal is to create a small, consistent container type to which components attach. Keep in mind: deciding whether something is a game object depends on whether it needs to be managed each frame; if not, it may be plain data rather than an entity.

Inheritance gives a natural “is-a” relationship, which is useful in many domains. In games, however, inheritance often creates brittle trees: a Player needs inventory, an Enemy needs AI, and a Tree might need collision. If you rely on inheritance, you quickly face either duplication or a bloated base class that tries to do everything. Composition solves this by attaching small, focused components to a generic GameObject container. For example, a Player can have Position, Render, Input, and Health components while a Tree only has Position and Render. The advantage is flexibility: add a Flight component and any entity can fly without changing an inheritance hierarchy. A common disadvantage is the need for component lookup and interaction: for instance, MovementComponent must find PositionComponent to update coordinates. That adds some bookkeeping, like passing a parent pointer or using GetComponent checks. A balanced understanding is important: use composition for flexible, varied entities, but design clear interaction patterns so components can find and communicate with each other without fragile assumptions. Composition vs Inheritance means composition yields modular, reusable behavior; avoid deep inheritance that forces a monolithic base class or many specialized subclasses.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Component base class establishes the contract every concrete component follows. The example uses a virtual destructor so derived components clean up properly when deleted through a base pointer. It also defines virtual Update and Render functions; Update is usually pure virtual because most components implement per-frame logic, while Render can be optional. Finally, a GetTypeName method helps identify components when printing or logging. In C++ this base class is intentionally small to let concrete components focus on data and behavior. For instance, PositionComponent owns x and y coordinates and does not render, while RenderComponent holds a sprite name and implements Render. The code pattern uses std::unique_ptr to manage component lifetimes inside a GameObject, which prevents leaks and centralizes ownership. A common misconception is that components must be heavyweight objects; instead they should be minimal and composable. The GameObject in this chapter is intentionally simple: it owns a vector of std::unique_ptr and provides template helpers AddComponent and GetComponent.
